His body is smooth, well-proportioned, clean, soft, and pure;
His distinguishing marks are complete; his body is beautiful, broad, and well-rounded. (Abhis 8.23)
His steps are even; his eyes are pure and delicate;
His body is neither dejected nor raised excessively, and his limbs are well-knit and compact. (Abhis 8.24)
His limbs are well-proportioned; his vision is clear, dispelling darkness and purified;
His belly is round, smooth, unblemished, not sunken, and deep. (Abhis 8.25)
His navel spirals to the right; he is pleasing to behold from all sides;
His conduct is proper; his body is pure, free from marks of moles and blemishes. (Abhis 8.26)
His hands are soft like cotton, glossy, with lines that are deep and extended;
His speech is not overly prolonged; his lips are like the <s>bimba</s> fruit and its reflection. (Abhis 8.27)

children.text: mṛdvī tanvī ca raktā ca jihvā jīmūtaghoṣatā /
children.translated_text: His tongue is soft, slender, and red; his voice is like the rumbling of thunderclouds;

children.text: cārumañjusvaro daṃṣṭrā vṛttāstīkṣṇāḥ sitāḥ samāḥ // Abhis_8.28 //
children.translated_text: His voice is sweet and melodious; his canine teeth are round, sharp, white, and even. (Abhis 8.28)
His teeth taper gradually and are prominent; his nose is supremely clean;
His eyes are wide, with thick lashes, and are marked like the petals of a lotus. (Abhis 8.29)
His eyebrows and arms are long, smooth, well-oiled, even in hair;
His ears are full and extended, even, and free from impairment. (Abhis 8.30)
His forehead is unwrinkled; his head is broad, full, and excellent;
His hair is thick as a bee-swarm, smooth, with locks that are not disheveled. (Abhis 8.31)
His hair is not coarse, and its fragrance captivates people;
The <s>Śrīvatsa</s> and the <s>Svastika</s> — these are considered the <s>anuvyañjana</s>s (minor marks) of the <s>Buddha</s>. (Abhis 8.32)
Thus: (1) Through being free from attachment to all <s>saṃskāra</s>s (conditioned formations), there is the mark of copper-colored nails.

(2) Through the intention to benefit all sentient beings, glossy nails.
(3) Through originating from a noble lineage, prominent nails.
(4) Through blameless conduct, rounded fingers.

4 - The <s>Nairmāṇikakāya</s> (Emanation Body)

children.text:
itthaṃ kāyatrayaṃ nirdiśyaṃ caturthaḥ nairmāṇikakāyaḥ sarvabālajanasādhāraṇa iti /
tamāha -
children.translated_text: Having thus described the three bodies, the fourth, the <s>Nairmāṇikakāya</s> (Emanation Body), is common to all ordinary beings. [The author] states this:

children.text: karoti yena citrāṇi hitāni jagataḥ samam /
children.translated_text: "By which he performs various beneficial deeds for the world equally,
uninterrupted throughout existence—that is the <s>Nairmāṇikakāya</s> (Emanation Body) of the Sage." (Abhis 8.33)

children.text: iti / yena śākyamunitathāgatādirūpeṇa āsaṃsāraṃ sarvalokadhātuṣu sattvānāṃ samīhitamarthaṃ samaṃ karoti, asau kāyaḥ prabandhatayā anuparato nairmāṇiko buddhasya bhagavataḥ sarvabālajanasādhāraṇaścaturtho 'vasātavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus: That body which, in the form of <s>Tathāgatas</s> such as <s>Śākyamuni</s>, equally accomplishes the desired aims of sentient beings in all world-realms throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>—that unceasing body, by way of continuity, is the <s>Nairmāṇikakāya</s> (Emanation Body) of the <s>Buddha Bhagavān</s>, common to all ordinary beings, and is to be understood as the fourth.
<s>Buddhakāritras</s> (Buddha-Activities)

children.text: ityevaṃ svābhāvikakāyasvarūpabhāvanāprabhāvitabuddhādiviṣayatve jñānādyapekṣya parikalpitakāyatrayaṃ nirdiśyaṃ saṃvṛtyā jñānameva sāmbhogikakāyādipratibhāsotpādadvāreṇārthakriyākārīti karma vineyajanapratibhāsabhāk tadādhipatyāśrayeṇāyātaṃ dharmakāya eveti /
children.translated_text: Thus, having described the three conceptually designated bodies with respect to the <s>Svābhāvikakāya</s> (Essential Body) whose nature is cultivated through meditation on the Buddha-realm and other objects, in dependence upon wisdom and the rest, conventionally it is wisdom itself that performs activity through the door of producing the appearance of the <s>Sāmbhogikakāya</s> (Enjoyment Body) and so forth. The activity, being a share of the appearance to those to be trained, comes about through the dominant condition—and thus it belongs to the <s>Dharmakāya</s> alone.
"Likewise, its activity is considered unceasing throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>:

children.text: gatīnāṃ śamanaṃ karma saṅgrahe ca caturvidhe // Abhis_8.34 //
children.translated_text: The pacification of the [lower] destinies is its activity, as is [establishing beings] in the fourfold means of gathering [disciples]," (Abhis 8.34)
"establishing them in [understanding] the afflicted and the purified,
in the true nature of the aims of sentient beings, and in the six <s>pāramitās</s> (perfections);" (Abhis 8.35)
"in the path of the <s>Buddha</s>, in the natural emptiness, in the cessation of duality,

children.text: saṃkete 'nupalambhe ca paripāke ca dehinām // Abhis_8.36 //
children.translated_text: in conventional designation, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of embodied beings;" (Abhis 8.36)
"in the path of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, in the prevention of attachment,
in the attainment of <s>Bodhi</s> (awakening), in the purification of the <s>Buddha</s>-fields, and with respect to certainty;" (Abhis 8.37)
"in the immeasurable welfare of sentient beings, in qualities such as service to the <s>Buddhas</s>,
in the non-destruction of the limbs of awakening, and in the perception of truth with respect to actions;" (Abhis 8.38)
"in the abandonment of inverted views, in the approach of the unreality of those [inversions],
in purification together with its accumulations, and with respect to the conditioned and the unconditioned;" (Abhis 8.39)
"in the cognition of the non-differentiation, and the establishment in <s>Nirvāṇa</s>—
this activity of the <s>Dharmakāya</s> is considered to be twenty-seven-fold." (Abhis 8.40)

children.text: iti / tatra prathamaṃ praśastāpraśastagatyanabhiniveśāvasthānalakṣaṇaṃ gatipraśamanaṃ karma kṛtvā, dānādicatuḥsaṅgrahavastuni pratiṣṭhāpya, śrutamayādijñānena vipakṣapratipakṣaheyopādeyadvāreṇa bodhayitvā, māyākāra ivānunayādiviviktatayā maitryādilakṣaṇe parārthe sattvārthayāthātmye pratiṣṭhāpya, tadanu svārthe trimaṇḍalaviśuddhiprabhāvitaṣaṭpāramitābhyāse, tadanantaraṃ svaparārthalakṣaṇe daśakuśalakarmapathe buddhamārge, tataḥ sarvadharmaprakṛtiśūnyatābhyāse, tadanu dānapāramitādhiṣṭhānena prathamāyāṃ bhūmau sarvatragadharmadhātuprativedhalakṣaṇe advayadharme, tato dvitīyādibhūmau sambhāraparipūrihetubhūte śīlādipāramitāsarvadharmasāṅketikajñāne niveśayati / evamanukrameṇa prajñāpāramitādhiṣṭhānena ṣaṣṭhyāṃ bhūmau jñānajñeyabhāvānabhiniveśalakṣaṇe sarvadharmānupalambhe, tadanantaraṃ saptamyāmupāyapāramitābalena sattvaparipāke, tato balapāramitābalenāṣṭamyāṃ śrāvakādyasādhāraṇe bodhisattvamārge, punastatraiva sarvabhāvābhiniveśaprahāṇe, tadanu navamyāṃ praṇidhānapāramitāsāmarthyād bodhiprāptau, tadanantaraṃ jñānapāramitābalād daśamyāṃ bhūmau vividhabuddhakṣetraviśuddhau pratiṣṭhāpya, punastatraiva ekajātipratibaddhasvarūpe samyak sambodhipratiniyame daśadiglokadhātavīyasattvārthe sarvalokadhātubuddhopasaṅkramaṇādiguṇe ca niveśayati /
children.translated_text: Thus: First, having performed the activity of pacifying the [lower] destinies, characterized by non-attachment to favorable and unfavorable states of existence, and having established [beings] in the four means of gathering beginning with generosity, and having awakened them through knowledge born of learning and the rest by way of the antidotes to adversaries and what is to be abandoned and adopted, and having established them in the true nature of the aims of sentient beings—characterized by <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) and the rest for the benefit of others, being detached from attraction and so forth like a magician—then, for one's own benefit, in the practice of the six <s>pāramitās</s> empowered by the purity of the three spheres, and next, in the path of the <s>Buddha</s> on the tenfold wholesome course of action characterized by the benefit of self and others, then in the practice of the natural emptiness of all <s>dharmas</s>, then through the empowerment of the <s>Dānapāramitā</s> (perfection of giving) on the first <s>bhūmi</s> (stage) in the non-dual <s>Dharma</s> characterized by the penetration of the all-pervading <s>dharmadhātu</s>, then from the second <s>bhūmi</s> onward, [the <s>Dharmakāya</s>] establishes [beings] in the conventional knowledge of all <s>dharmas</s> through the <s>pāramitās</s> beginning with <s>Śīla</s> (morality), which serve as causes for the fulfillment of the accumulations. In this same sequence, through the empowerment of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> (perfection of wisdom) on the sixth <s>bhūmi</s>, in the non-apprehension of all <s>dharmas</s> characterized by non-attachment to the nature of knower and knowable; then on the seventh [<s>bhūmi</s>], through the power of <s>Upāyapāramitā</s> (perfection of skillful means), in the maturation of sentient beings; then through the power of <s>Balapāramitā</s> (perfection of power) on the eighth [<s>bhūmi</s>], in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> path uncommon with <s>Śrāvakas</s> and others; and again there, in the abandonment of attachment to all existents; then on the ninth [<s>bhūmi</s>], through the power of <s>Praṇidhānapāramitā</s> (perfection of aspiration), in the attainment of <s>Bodhi</s>; then through the power of <s>Jñānapāramitā</s> (perfection of wisdom) on the tenth <s>bhūmi</s>, having established [beings] in the purification of various <s>Buddha</s>-fields; and again there, [the <s>Dharmakāya</s>] establishes [beings] in the welfare of sentient beings of the world-realms in the ten directions—in the form of being bound to one more birth—in the certainty of perfect complete awakening, and in the qualities of approaching the <s>Buddhas</s> of all world-realms.

children.text: evamanukrameṇa punastatraina viśeṣamārgasvarūpe samastabodhyāvāhakadharmalakṣaṇe bodhyaṅge, karmaphalasambandhāvipraṇāśe, yathābhūtapadārthādhigame, sarvaviparyāsaprahāṇe, nirvastukaviparyāsaprahāṇe jñāne, prakṛtipariśuddhilakṣaṇe bodhisattvavyavadāne, sarvakalaṅkāpagatavyavadānahetau sambhāre, śūnyatāsvabhāvena saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛtāvyatibhedaparijñāne ca pratiṣṭhāpya tāthāgatyāṃ bhūmau nirvāṇe niveśayati / evaṃ dharmakāyavadasya saptaviṃśatiprakāraṃ karma āsaṃsāramiṣyata iti kāritram /
children.translated_text: In this same sequence, again there, in the <s>bodhyaṅgas</s> (limbs of awakening) characterized by the <s>Dharma</s> that brings about complete awakening, being of the nature of the special path; in the non-destruction of the connection between actions and their fruits; in the realization of things as they truly are; in the abandonment of all inverted views; in the knowledge of the abandonment of baseless inverted views; in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> purification characterized by natural purity; in the accumulations that are the cause of purification free from all stains; and having established [beings] in the cognition of the non-differentiation of the conditioned and the unconditioned by their nature of emptiness, [the <s>Dharmakāya</s>] establishes [beings] in <s>Nirvāṇa</s> on the <s>Tathāgata</s> stage. Thus, like the <s>Dharmakāya</s> itself, its twenty-seven types of activity are considered to continue throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>—such is the <s>kāritra</s> (Buddha-activity).

children.text: prathamacittotpādasya antimakarmaṇāñca anukramanirdeśena avaśiṣṭānāṃ madhyapadārthānāmapi kramo veditavyaḥ, vaktavyabāhulyabhayānmayā nollikhitaḥ /
children.translated_text: From the sequential exposition of the first generation of <s>bodhicitta</s> (awakening mind) and the final activities, the order of the intermediate topics that remain should also be understood; I have not written them out due to the fear of excessive verbosity.
Thus concludes the commentary on the eighth chapter of the <s>Abhisamayālaṃkāra</s>, the treatise on the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>.
Explanation for Beings of Middling Inclination

children.text: evaṃ vistararucisattvānugraheṇa aṣṭabhiḥ padārthaiḥ (prajñāpāramitāṃ) vyākhyāya punaranyaprakāreṇa vyākhyānāyāha -
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s> by means of eight topics for the benefit of beings who delight in elaborate exposition, [the author] now states another mode of explanation:
"The characteristic, its practice, its excellence, its sequence,
its culmination, and its fruition—this is the alternative sixfold summary of meaning." (1)

children.text: iti / prathamaṃ sarvākārajñatāditrisarvajñatābhilakṣyasthānīyatvena lakṣaṇam / tato vaśitvārthatrisarvajñatābhāvanāṃ prati prayujyate 'neneti trisarvajñatāprayogaḥ sarvākārābhisambodhaḥ / tato 'tyabhyāsāt prakarṣagamanamiti trisarvajñatāyāḥ prakarṣāvasthomūrdhābhisamayaḥ / tato 'dhigatavastuniścayāya vyastasamastavibhāvitārthapraguṇīkaraṇamiti trisarvajñatānukramāvastho 'nupūrvābhisamayaḥ / tato viśeṣagamanābhāvāt trisarvajñatāniṣṭhāvasthaḥ samyagekakṣaṇābhisambodhaḥ / tatastasya phalam, iti trisarvajñatāvipāko dharmakāyaḥ sakāritraḥ / evaṃ ṣaṭprakāreṇārthasaṃgraheṇa pūrvavadeva jinajananī vyākhyeyā /
children.translated_text: Thus: First, being the intended object of the three kinds of omniscience beginning with <s>Sarvākārajñatā</s> (knowledge of all aspects), this is the 'characteristic.' Then, that by which one engages in the cultivation of the three kinds of omniscience for the purpose of mastery is the 'practice of the three kinds of omniscience'—namely, the <s>Sarvākārābhisambodha</s> (realization of all aspects). Then, through intensive cultivation, there is the attainment of excellence—the culminating stage of the three kinds of omniscience, the <s>Mūrdhābhisamaya</s> (peak realization). Then, for the ascertainment of the realized object, the sequential refinement of the meaning through individual and combined contemplation is the stage of the sequence of the three kinds of omniscience—the <s>Anupūrvābhisamaya</s> (gradual realization). Then, because there is no further progress, the culminating stage of the three kinds of omniscience is the <s>Ekakṣaṇābhisambodha</s> (realization in a single instant). Then its fruit—the ripening of the three kinds of omniscience—is the <s>Dharmakāya</s> together with its activities. Thus, by means of a sixfold summary of meaning, the Mother of the Conquerors is to be explained in the same manner as before.
Explanation for Beings of Concise Inclination

children.text: madhyamarucisattvānukampayā amunā ṣaṭprakāreṇārthasaṃgraheṇa vyākhyāya punaḥ saṃkṣiptarucisattvānurodhenānyaprakāreṇa vyākhyānāyāha -
children.translated_text: Having explained by means of this sixfold summary of meaning out of compassion for beings of middling inclination, [the author] now states another mode of explanation in accordance with beings who delight in conciseness:
"The threefold object, the cause, the fourfold practice,
the <s>Dharmakāya</s> as the fruit, and the activity—this is the alternative threefold summary of meaning." (2)

children.text: iti / ādau sarvākārajñatāditrisarvajñatāsvabhāvaḥ pravṛttiviṣayahetuḥ / sa kathaṃ prayujyata iti tadanantaraṃ sarvākārābhisambodhādiścaturvidho 'bhisamayaḥ prayogaḥ / tasyaivaṃ prayogavato viṣayasya kiṃ phalamiti tadanu dharmakāyaḥ sakarmā phalamityevaṃ trividhenārthasaṃgraheṇa tathaiva jinajananī vyākhyeyā /
children.translated_text: Thus: First, the object-cause of engagement, having the nature of the three kinds of omniscience beginning with <s>Sarvākārajñatā</s> (knowledge of all aspects). Then, how is it practiced?—following that, the fourfold <s>abhisamaya</s> (realization) beginning with <s>Sarvākārābhisambodha</s> (realization of all aspects) is the 'practice.' What is the fruit of that object which is thus practiced?—following that, the <s>Dharmakāya</s> together with its activities is the 'fruit.' Thus, by means of a threefold summary of meaning, the Mother of the Conquerors is to be explained in the same manner.
Dedication
"In meaning, in word, or in synonym—
just this much is to be known by the wise as the summary meaning in all the Mother [<s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>] texts." (1)
Otherwise there would not be a correct sequential inclusion of all [the topics].
Therein, through the distinctions of summary and so forth, the special features certainly arise.
Through the power of Noble <s>Vimuktisena</s>, here is shown
the meaning alone, for the sake of easy understanding, having omitted the verbosity of the words.
Having bowed to my <s>guru</s> <s>Vairocana</s>, the knower [who is] a true preceptor,
a clear commentary (<s>vṛtti</s>) on the <s>kārikās</s> is composed by <s>Haribhadra</s>.
By the merit I have acquired through the composition of this treatise,
may all living beings attain the wisdom of the <s>Sugata</s> (the <s>Buddha</s>).
Where am I, a man of little intelligence, standing outside all the <s>śāstras</s>?
And where is this meaning of the <s>śāstra</s>, possessed of greatness, accessible only to the Noble Ones' scope?
Nevertheless, though it lies beyond my reach, I have made an effort,
solely with the thought of benefiting others and myself—may the virtuous forgive this.

children.text: aho mṛśaṃ mayā nānāmataiḥ śrāntena vīkṣitam /
children.translated_text: Ah, I have examined in vain, wearied by various doctrines,
and at last this place of peace has been found—the doctrine of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>.

Thus the <s>Abhisamayālaṃkāravṛtti</s> (Commentary on the Ornament of Clear Realization), composed by <s>Ācārya Haribhadra</s>, in the Instructional Treatise on the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>, is completed.

children.text:
bhāratīyapaṇḍitena vidyākaraprabheṇa mahālokacakṣuṣā vandeśrīkūṭena cānūdya nirṇītā /
śrīpaṇḍitāmaragomyādibhiḥ bhikṣudhīmatprajñena ca paścāt sunirṇītā /
children.translated_text: It was translated and established by the Indian <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Vidyākaraprabha</s>, the great eye of the world, together with <s>Bande Śrīkūṭa</s>. Later it was well-established by the illustrious <s>paṇḍitas</s> <s>Amaragomi</s> and others, together with the monk <s>Dhīmatprajña</s>.
